papers.title: Rac1-Abi-1 Signaling Links DNA Repair to Tumorigenesis
papers.abstract: The DNA damage response governs genomic integrity, and abnormal DNA repair can drive tumorigenesis. We previously identified a Rac1-Abi-1 signaling pathway in which Rac1 activates protein phosphatase 5, leading to Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation and enhanced non-homologous end joining (NHEJ). Given the error-prone nature of NHEJ and its potential to promote genomic instability, we sought to determine whether Rac1-Abi-1-mediated regulation of NHEJ contributes to tumorigenesis. Here, we demonstrate the tumorigenic role of Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation in nonmalignant cell models and multiple tumorigenesis models established using a newly generated genetically engineered Abi-1 mouse model. We first found that the dephospho-mimetic Abi-1-S323A mutant promoted transformation-associated phenotypes in nonmalignant human cells and enhanced orthotopic glioblastoma growth under unperturbed conditions. To further investigate its tumorigenic potential in vivo, we generated CRISPR/Cas9-mediated Abi-1-S296A knock-in mice, in which S296 corresponds to human S323. Abi-1-S296A mouse embryonic fibroblasts exhibited increased proliferation, while mutant mice developed spontaneous tumors involving lymphoid tissues and organs under unperturbed conditions. Furthermore, Abi-1-S296A increased susceptibility to tumorigenesis following DNA damage. In a low-dose whole-body irradiation model, Abi-1-S296A mice showed a trend toward shortened survival and increased tumor development, with lesions including Harderian gland papillary cystadenomas, round-cell neoplasms, and anaplastic sarcomas. In addition, in an azoxymethane/dextran sulfate sodium (AOM/DSS)-induced colorectal tumor model, Abi-1-S296A mice developed significantly more tumors and had a greater tumor burden. These findings identify Abi-1-S323 dephosphorylation as a previously unrecognized regulator of tumorigenesis and establish a new mouse model for investigating the physiological and pathological consequences of constitutive activation of upstream NHEJ-regulatory signaling.

papers.title: A near-infrared fluorescent genetically encoded calcium ion biosensor with a direct response
papers.abstract: Near-infrared genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (NIR GECIs) enable Ca2+ imaging at longer wavelengths than green or red fluorescent GECIs, providing reduced autofluorescence and phototoxicity, and improved compatibility with deep-tissue and multiplexed imaging applications. We have previously reported biliverdin (BV)-binding phytochrome-based NIR GECIs such as NIR-GECO2G that exhibit inverse fluorescence responses. Although inverse response GECIs can effectively report Ca2+ dynamics, their high baseline fluorescence in the resting apo state causes faster photobleaching and substantial out-of-focus background fluorescence, complicating signal interpretation. Here, using the inverse response NIR-GECO2G as the starting scaffold, we developed a direct response Ca2+ indicator, designated dNIR-GECO1.0, through iterative rounds of protein engineering and screening. dNIR-GECO1.0 exhibited greater molecular brightness than NIR-GECO2G, robust fluorescence in mammalian cells without exogenous BV supplementation, and a high dynamic range for reporting Ca2+ changes. A detailed mechanistic investigation identified the key mutations within the Ca2+ binding domain that were necessary to convert the inverse response indicator into a direct response indicator. Resonance Raman spectroscopic analysis provided insight into the specific changes in the BV chromophore resulting from the Ca2+-dependent conformational change.

papers.title: Metabolic transitions reprogram translation through sequence-dependent regulation
papers.abstract: Cells suppress protein synthesis during starvation, but how translation recovers upon nutrient repletion remains poorly understood. To address this gap, we followed translational recovery in budding yeast after repletion of glucose, nitrogen, or phosphate, combining time-resolved metabolomics, structural proteomics, transcriptomics, and spike-in-calibrated ribosome profiling. Nutrient addition rapidly altered ribosome occupancy in distinct, transcript-specific programs. To identify their sequence determinants, we developed RiboNet, a deep learning framework that predicts ribosome load and positions along transcripts from mRNA sequence. RiboNet-guided in silico mutagenesis revealed reduced pausing at serine codons upon glucose repletion and transiently increased pausing at leucine codons following nitrogen repletion. These responses coincided with altered cognate tRNA charging and metabolite-associated structural changes in aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases. RiboNet also identified a conserved 5' UTR motif, GAUY, that increased reporter protein output following glucose repletion. Our findings reveal how metabolic state alters the contributions of mRNA sequence features to translation initiation and elongation.

papers.title: Native architecture of a mitochondrial oxphosome
papers.abstract: Mitochondrial cristae are the primary bioenergetic units of eukaryotic cells, yet the molecular principles that dictate their morphologies remain largely unknown. Using in situ cryo-electron tomography and integrative modeling, we resolve the native organization of the respiratory machinery in the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum. Unlike previously studied animals and green algae, diatoms possess tubular crista, a conserved membrane architecture found in diverse and globally relevant species. We identify several native supercomplexes assemblies, including an oxphosome comprising the entire respiratory chain. Our results, together with molecular dynamics analyses, reveal that these supercomplexes assemble through a lipid-mediated mechanism. We propose that tubular cristae are shaped by the interplay between membrane-bending ATP synthase oligomers that bud the hemispherical crista tips and supercomplexes that act as molecular roadblocks to constrain ATP synthase propagation, thereby balancing membrane curvature and allowing cristae body extension. Furthermore, we show that the diatom Complex I retains ancestral subunits related to fatty acid synthase. Beyond illuminating diatom bioenergetics, our findings reveal a fundamental principle of mitochondrial morphogenesis where ATP synthase-driven membrane curvature is spatially fine-tuned by respiratory supercomplexes.

papers.title: LANCE-seq: Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction for Spatial Transcriptomics
papers.abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the resolution of spatial heterogeneity in gene expression within tissues, yet most existing sequencing-based methods rely on ex vivo tissue processing, making it difficult to track dynamic molecular changes in the same living individual. We developed LANCE-seq (Live-tissue Analysis via Needle-encoded Capture Extraction sequencing), a live-tissue spatial transcriptomics platform based on encoded microneedle arrays that enables high-density spatial RNA capture through poly(amidoamine) (PAMAM) dendrimer-functionalized interfaces and microfluidic orthogonal combinatorial encoding. In frozen mouse brain tissue, LANCE-seq detected an average of 6,399 genes per spatial spot and reconstructed the spatial distribution of major brain regions and representative marker genes. Furthermore, in the acetaminophen (APAP)-induced acute liver injury model, LANCE-seq enabled repeated sampling from the same living animal at different time points. At 6 h after APAP treatment, injury-related genes such as Hmox1, Ddit3, Atf3, and Fgf21 were significantly elevated, and transcriptional programs associated with stress, inflammation, and cellular injury were broadly enhanced. Meanwhile, liver zonation-related transcriptional signatures were remodeled, with different relative zonation states all exhibiting activation of injury programs. By integrating high-throughput spatial encoding with minimally invasive in vivo sampling, LANCE-seq provides a platform for longitudinal spatial transcriptomic studies of drug responses and disease progression.

papers.title: PYTHOCHEMICAL COMPOSITION AND ANTIMICROBIAL ACTIVITY OF LEPIDIUM SATIVUM SEED EXTRACTS AGAINST SELECTED HUMAN PATHOGENS.
papers.abstract: This study evaluates the antimicrobial activity of Lepidium sativum (Garden Cress) seed extracts against Staphylococcus aureus, Escherichia coli, Fusarium oxysporum, and Candida albicans using methanol and acetone as solvents. The antimicrobial effects were assessed through the zone of inhibition and minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) using serial dilution. The methanol extract exhibited the highest inhibition zones, measuring 23.6 mm for S. aureus and 21.5 mm for E. coli, while the acetone extract showed 22.9 mm and 18.3 mm, respectively. C. albicans exhibited moderate susceptibility, with inhibition zones of 16.2 mm (methanol) and 14.8 mm (acetone), whereas F. oxysporum showed weaker inhibition at 12.4 mm and 10.7 mm, respectively. MIC values ranged from 10-1 to 10-4 dilutions, with methanol extracts maintaining higher efficacy at lower concentrations. These findings validate Lepidium sativum as a potential natural antimicrobial agent, particularly against gram-positive bacteria, and suggest further exploration of its bioactive compounds for pharmaceutical applications.

papers.title: Cumulative antibiograms: effects of isolate selection and stratification order on susceptibility estimates and resistance representation
papers.abstract: Cumulative antibiograms depend on how isolates are selected and how data are stratified. Different selection strategies may affect both the number of isolates included and the susceptibility estimates reported. We retrospectively analyzed routine microbiology records from a tertiary-care hospital in Barcelona, Spain (2022-2025). Within each patient-organism-calendar-year unit, we compared three isolate-selection strategies: first-isolate, resistance-phenotype, and susceptibility-profile. We assessed the number of isolates retained, susceptibility at standard or increased exposure, the identification of resistance-phenotype profiles, and the effect of de-duplication before versus after stratification. Annual differences in susceptibility were estimated using paired cluster-bootstrap confidence intervals. For Pseudomonas aeruginosa, susceptibility-profile selection retained 16.9% more isolates than first-isolate selection, with differences exceeding 5 percentage points in 10 of 44 annual antimicrobial comparisons. No annual susceptibility differences exceeding this threshold were observed for the other species. Resistance-phenotype and susceptibility-profile selection criteria identified 468 MDR and 278 XDR P. aeruginosa isolates. Of these, 90 (19.2%) of the MDR and 53 (19.1%) of the XDR isolates were not captured by first-isolate selection. In the broader stratification dataset, stratification-first processing increased first-isolate retention by 21.2% for blood specimens and 11.2% for inpatients. These findings show that modest changes in cumulative susceptibility can coexist with incomplete representation of resistant phenotypes. In conclusion, phenotype- and AST-profile-based selection capture additional resistance information beyond first-isolate selection, despite modest differences in cumulative susceptibility. Clinical validation is needed before their use to guide empirical therapy.

papers.title: Auditory bullae enlarge along an aridity gradient in a diverse subfamily of small carnivorous mammals
papers.abstract: The world`s arid regions are home to diverse assemblages of small mammals, many of which possess a range of physiological, behavioral, and sensory adaptations to the harsh selective pressures imposed by arid environments. The mammalian skull facilitates a range of sensory functions, meaning that arid-dwelling species likely possess distinct skull adaptations which have evolved in response to the unique selective pressures imposed by arid environments. Studies on arid-adapted rodents have highlighted hearing as being important for arid adaptation; however, the adaptive potential of the entire skull is rarely considered. Here, we used 3D geometric morphometrics to test for signatures of arid adaptation using 168 skulls across 30 species of the Sminthopsinae, a subfamily of small insectivorous marsupials, found across Australia. We found that relative bulla size increased by 20% along an aridity gradient from mesic to hyper arid. We also found that species further from the equator tended to have wider posterior nasal cavities, which may be related to selection for thermoregulatory capabilities. Our findings demonstrate the role of the skull in facilitating adaptation to aridity and provide further evidence that selection for improved low-frequency hearing appears to be a key driver of skull shape in arid-zone small mammals.

papers.title: Temperature and skn-1 determine whether developmental daf-2 knockdown extends C. elegans lifespan
papers.abstract: The evolutionarily conserved insulin/IGF-1 signalling pathway (IIS) shapes life-history traits largely through downstream transcription factors including SKN-1. Reduced IIS (rIIS) in adulthood robustly extends Caenorhabditis elegans lifespan, yet developmental rIIS has long been considered unable to extend lifespan and costly to fitness, a conclusion drawn almost entirely from experiments at 25{degrees}C, near the species' upper thermal limit. Here we knocked down daf-2 during development in wild-type and skn-1 loss-of-function nematodes across constant and fluctuating temperatures. Contrary to the prevailing view, developmental daf-2 knockdown extended lifespan at constant 15{degrees}C in both backgrounds, but not at 25{degrees}C, revealing that its late-life benefit is strongly temperature-dependent and, under constant conditions, independent of skn-1. Under daily 15-25{degrees}C cycling, developmental daf-2 knockdown again extended lifespan, but whether this required skn-1 was itself determined by the temperature experienced at the start of development. Lifespan extension was accompanied by condition-specific reproductive costs. Together, our results identify a developmental window in which IIS, skn-1 and temperature interact to set adult ageing trajectories and show that the thermal environment determines whether reducing IIS during development extends lifespan.

papers.title: Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and remodel host-cell metabolism
papers.abstract: Flaviviruses reprogram host-cell metabolism to support viral replication. In previous work, we showed that Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins inhibit dengue virus replication and were predicted to interact with viral enzymes. Here, we investigated whether S01, a purified solid from Solanum ovalifolium containing predominantly two characterized spirostane saponins, also modulates host-cell metabolism in association with reduced permissiveness to dengue virus serotype 2 (DENV-2). We performed untargeted GC-QTOF-MS metabolomics in Vero cells under four conditions, including untreated control, S01 treatment, DENV-2 infection, and DENV-2 infection with S01 treatment. Quality-control samples clustered tightly, supporting analytical reproducibility. Principal component analysis revealed separation among experimental groups, and PERMANOVA confirmed significant global metabolic differences (F = 27.567, R{superscript 2} = 0.827, p = 0.001). S01 also retained strong antiviral activity, producing 99.9% inhibition under the metabolomics conditions. DENV-2 infection was associated with alterations metabolites related to amino acid, carbohydrate, lipid, and sphingolipid metabolism. Pathway analysis highlighted glutamate metabolism, arginine and proline metabolism, glycolysis-related pathways, fatty-acid oxidation and carnitine-associated metabolism, phosphatidylcholine biosynthesis, and sphingolipid metabolism. In uninfected cells, S01 induced a distinct metabolic profile (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.951, Q{superscript 2} = 0.851; permutation p = 0.002), characterized by increased carbohydrate-related metabolites, including the unresolved Talose/D-glucose feature, gluconic acid, 2-keto-L-gulonic acid, and D-mannitol, together with decreased abundance of selected lipid-related metabolites. During infection, S01 induced a distinct metabolic (OPLS-DA R{superscript 2}Y = 0.928, Q{superscript 2} = 0.841), characterized by lower abundance of several fatty-acid-related and organic-acid metabolites and higher abundance of carbohydrate-related metabolites, while modifying selected DENV-2-associated metabolic alterations. These findings associate S01 antiviral activity with substantial remodeling of host-cell metabolism. Together with previous docking predictions of interactions with viral targets, the results support a model in which the antiviral activity of Solanaceae-derived spirostane saponins may involve complementary effects on viral and host-associated processes.

papers.title: The evolution of sexual dimorphism in the weapon system of leaf-footed bugs (Hemiptera: Coreoidea)
papers.abstract: The natural world contains an extraordinary diversity of morphologically elaborate traits, yet the evolutionary processes underlying the emergence and diversification of sexual dimorphism in these structures are not fully resolved. Some of the most extravagant of these traits are the mechanical weapons of sexual selection. They include such noteworthy structures as the tusks of narwals and the mandibles of stag beetles. Such traits are notoriously sexually dimorphic -- often elaborated in one sex while absent or reduced in the other sex. The mechanisms by which sexual dimorphism evolves in such traits is only just beginning to be understood. Existing macroevolutionary studies have examined simple structures or have simplified elaborate and complex weapons using binary coding or metrics, limiting the insights that can be gained. Here, we investigated the macroevolutionary dynamics of sexual dimorphism across 14 traits in bodies and complex, elaborate weaponry of leaf-footed bugs (Hemiptera: Coreoidea) using phylogenomic data and quantitative and qualitative trait analyses. Phylogenetic generalized linear mixed models across 27 species showed that females are generally larger-bodied, whereas males exhibit greater exaggeration in most putative weapon traits, often with steeper allometric scaling. Ancestral state estimation across 154 species revealed that sexual dimorphism is evolutionarily labile and heterogeneous across traits. Contrary to expectations from classical models, sexual dimorphism most commonly arose when new traits originated in both sexes already in a dimorphic state, rather than through subsequent divergence from ancestrally shared, monomorphic traits or as a sex-limited trait. At the level of entire weapon system, sexual dimorphism varied widely across lineages, clustered phylogenetically, and reached extreme levels through coordinated changes across multiple traits. By showing that complex weapon systems diversify through semi-independent changes and that new traits often arise already dimorphic, our study highlights the need for further studies on the developmental mechanisms of sexual dimorphism, how weapon traits covary within and between sexes, and the relative roles of different selective pressures in shaping weapon systems.

papers.title: Contingency and determinism in rapid adaptation shape evolutionary rescue and extinction in Drosophila
papers.abstract: Populations declining under anthropogenic stressors, including rising temperatures and novel chemicals, may depend on rapid adaptation to persist. Yet fundamental questions remain about what promotes and constrains such evolutionary rescue. We tracked demographic, phenotypic, and genomic dynamics in a replicated outdoor evolution experiment using Drosophila under insecticide stress, and also manipulated initial maladaptation by pre-adapting a subset of populations. Half of populations without pre-adaptation went extinct and, unexpectedly, extinction was associated with a greater magnitude of phenotypic and parallel genomic adaptation. Rescue was driven by polygenic adaptation that was parallel across replicates and not predictable from genes previously implicated in insecticide resistance, with notable genomic convergence towards pre-adapted populations. Targeted intervention through pre-adaptation prevented extinction entirely, despite evidence of pleiotropic costs. Without intervention, evolutionary rescue remains contingent even with exceptionally rapid adaptation.

papers.title: Pioneering Hybrid Genome Assemblies of Fusarium graminearum and Fusarium avenaceum from Indian Wheat: Insights into Virulence Frameworks and Genome Evolution
papers.abstract: Fusarium head blight (FHB), primarily caused by various species of Fusarium, is a destructive disease of wheat that reduces yield and contaminates grain with mycotoxins. The present study reports high-quality hybrid genome assemblies for two Indian wheat isolates, Fusarium graminearum strain TNW1 and Fusarium avenaceum strain DMW8, representing the first genome-scale comparative study of FHB associated Fusarium isolates infectious on wheat from India. Both Indian isolates retained conserved Fusarium secondary metabolite clusters, including aurofusarin, chrysogine, clavaric acid, koraiol, orcinol/orsellinic acid, and oxyjavanicin, while exhibiting distinct species-associated biosynthetic profiles. TNW1 contained zearalenone and DON-related biosynthetic clusters, whereas DMW8 contained beauvericin and other species -associated clusters, highlighting differences in predicted biosynthetic potential between the two Fusarium species. Notably, both genomes showed relatively low transposable-element (TE) content compared with their respective species groups, with TEs occupying 0.96% of the TNW1 genome and 1.55% of the DMW8 genome. RIP-associated genomic coverage was also comparatively low, at 20.01% and 22.38%, respectively. TE insertion analysis identified predominantly reference-associated insertions, with two candidate non-reference insertions detected in DMW8. Gene-family analyses revealed greater duplication and expansion contraction dynamics in DMW8 than in TNW1. Together, these findings highlight differences in predicted genomic features, secondary metabolite biosynthetic potential, and gene family composition between the two Indian isolates, providing genomic resources for future investigations of Fusarium biology and wheat pathogen interactions.

papers.title: How good a predictor the in vitro antibiogram is, of in vivo antibiotic efficacy? An in vitro - in vivo integrated approach
papers.abstract: Conventional antimicrobial susceptibility testing, particularly the disc diffusion assay (DDA), provides a convenient means of assessing bacterial susceptibility to antibiotics. However, its ability to predict antibiotic efficacy in an infected host remains uncertain. This study investigated the relationship between DDA-derived inhibition zones and host-protective antibiotic activity using Caenorhabditis elegans infection models involving three bacterial pathogens: methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), Pseudomonas aeruginosa, and Clostridioides difficile. A total of 42 antibiotics were evaluated through DDA, while a separate panel of 75 antibiotics was screened using an automated C. elegans infection assay. Twenty-six antibiotics common to both panels were selected for comparative analysis. Gnotobiotic L3-L4 stage worms were challenged with individual pathogens in the presence of each antibiotic at a fixed concentration of 9.6 microgram/mL. Worm activity was quantified at 24, 48, and 72 h using an automated worm tracker system, with appropriate health, infection, vehicle, and antibiotic-toxicity controls. Overall, DDA-derived zone of inhibition (ZOI) diameters showed weak-to-moderate, pathogen- and time-dependent correlations with worm activity. At 24 h, Pearson's correlation coefficients ranged from -0.20 to 0.31 across the three pathogen-host systems, while at 48 h they ranged from -0.009 to 0.49. Notably, antibiotic rankings based on DDA and host-protective activity differed considerably. For example, against C. difficile, imipenem produced the largest inhibition zone (41 mm) but failed to protect worms at 24 and 48 h, whereas tobramycin, despite producing a smaller inhibition zone (26 mm), exhibited the highest early worm activity. Similar discrepancies were observed with the other pathogens. These findings demonstrate that DDA-derived susceptibility profiles do not consistently predict antibiotic-mediated protection in an infected host. The C. elegans model may therefore serve as a complementary whole-organism screening platform, providing additional functional information for prioritizing antimicrobial agents beyond conventional in vitro susceptibility testing.

papers.title: Intracellular spirochete integrates into a chemosynthetic micro-consortium of a deep-sea vent mussel
papers.abstract: Animal-microbe interactions comprise a diverse functional landscape, spanning pathogenic to mutualistic outcomes across extracellular and intracellular niches. Within this context, spirochetes are predominantly documented as extracellular associates or transient pathogens, leaving stable, functional endosymbiosis within animal cells unverified. Here, we report the discovery of an intracellular consortium comprising a spirochete and a primary sulfur-oxidizing bacterium within gill bacteriocytes of the deep-sea hydrothermal vent mussel Gigantidas horikoshii. Combining three-dimensional ultrastructural imaging, spatial histology, and multi-omics analyses, we characterize the intracellular spatial architecture and metabolic integration of this system. Both bacteria co-reside within a closed, membrane-bound network of interconnected chambers, where the spirochete is distributed across compartments and occasionally extends across host cell boundaries. Multi-omics profiling uncovers metabolic cooperation between the two bacteria: while the sulfur-oxidizing bacterium provides autotrophic primary production, the spirochete actively transcribes pathways for reactive oxygen species scavenging and organic acid assimilation, likely mitigating localized oxidative stress and acidosis. Coupled with its motility machinery and an expanded repertoire of host-interaction factors, these physiological traits suggest that the spirochete acts as an active stabilizer of the shared intracellular microenvironment. Together, these findings reveal that spirochetes can establish a stable, functional micro-consortium with chemosynthetic bacteria within animal cells, refining the recognized landscape of animal-microbe interactions and illuminating mechanisms linking mutualistic endosymbiosis and intracellular infections.

papers.title: Effect of neuB deletion on biofilm formation and extracellular electron transfer in Geobacter sulfurreducens
papers.abstract: The extracellular matrix of Geobacter sulfurreducens biofilms is primarily composed of proteins and exopolysaccharides. The extracellular polymeric substances (EPS) matrix provides the structural scaffold necessary to facilitate extracellular electron transfer (EET); however, the specific role of its carbohydrate components remains unexplored. Sialic acids are a class of carbohydrate derivates that can modulate extracellular matrix stability in bacteria. N-acetylneuraminic acid (Neu5Ac), the most common sialic acid, is primarily synthesized by NeuB. We hypothesized that the neuB gene homolog in G. sulfurreducens (gsu1970), putatively involved in Neu5Ac synthesis, plays a key role in EPS organization and EET performance. Deletion of neuB reduced insoluble Fe(III) oxide reduction by approximately 91%. Furthermore, confocal laser scanning microscopy (CLSM) revealed that the {Delta}neuB strain formed significantly less dense EPS matrices on both hematite and fluorine-doped tin oxide (FTO) electrodes. Interestingly, bioelectrochemical analysis of FTO anodes showed that the mutant produced a 3-fold higher current density and exhibited a more negative open-circuit potential than the wild-type strain. It is important to mention that this enhanced performance on FTO is linked to a significant upregulation of omcS, however, more specific experiments need to be performed to establish a definitive causal relationship between omcS transcription levels and the observed bioelectrochemical enhancement. This transcriptional change was not observed during growth on hematite. Our results suggest that neuB expression contributes to maintaining the structural integrity of the WGA-reactive glycoconjugates within the EPS matrix during insoluble iron reduction. Conversely, its absence is associated with a compensatory upregulation of omcS on FTO electrodes. Overall, this study highlights the potential importance of putative sialic acids-related biosynthetic pathways in Desulfuromonadia, showing that alteration of EPS carbohydrate biosynthetic genes can markedly influence both iron reduction and the performance of electroactive biofilms behavior.

papers.title: A metacommunity of complex microbial communities shows high spatial synchrony, ecological memory, gradual succession and invasion resistance
papers.abstract: Complex microbial communities are increasingly applied in biotechnological and health-related environments, yet maintaining their diversity and relative community composition over extended periods remains challenging. While dispersal can counteract the divergence of spatially separated communities, it remains unclear whether controlled mass transfer can sustain compositional synchrony in highly diverse communities over extended periods, whether this synchrony persist after dispersal is interrupted, and how robust such communities are to invasion. Here, we investigate these questions using a loop-design reactor (LDR) comprising five local wastewater microbial communities connected by controlled mass transfer. The experiment covered multiple rounds of alternating mass transfer and insular phases over a time frame of 318 days, different mass transfer intensities, and the introduction of defined microbial invaders. Community dynamics were monitored at a high temporal resolution by single-cell flow cytometry and complemented by metagenomic analyses of selected samples to characterize taxonomic compositions and functional potential. A Bray-Curtis-based Synchrony Index revealed that controlled mass transfer established high compositional synchrony among five local communities, which persisted for more than 150 generations. Although the community structures underwent gradual succession, the local communities remained synchronized, demonstrating parallel rather than divergent temporal trajectories. Interruption of dispersal initially promote divergence, whereas during later insular phases high compositional similarity persisted in the absence of mass transfer, consistent with ecological memory. Introduced microbial species failed to establish within resident communities, indicating high invasion resistance. Community functional potential remained largely stable throughout the experiment, although phosphorus accumulation failed during phases of high mass transfer. Together, these findings demonstrate that controlled mass transfer can maintain long-term spatial synchrony of complex microbial communities while allowing gradual community succession. Repeated connectivity promoted compositional similarity beyond periods of active dispersal while maintaining invasion resistance and functional stability, highlighting controlled dispersal as a promising community-level strategy for managing complex microbial communities.

papers.title: Genomes to Fields 2026: Genomic resources for investigating genotype-phenotype relationships in Zea mays
papers.abstract: Maize (Zea mays L.) is a major global crop characterized by high genetic and phenotypic diversity across accessions. To better understand this diversity, the Genomes-to-Fields initiative has produced paired genotypic and phenotypic datasets annually since 2014. Here, we present 15 genome assemblies representing 13 maize lines, including founders and testers from the 2022-2023, 2024-2025, and 2026-2027 Genomes-to-Fields evaluation cycles and additional breeding germplasm, together with gene and repeat annotations. Assemblies ranged from 2.19 to 2.38 Gb, with BUSCO completeness of 97.9-99.0%. Excluding the more fragmented LH287 assembly (contig N50 = 5.3 Mb; 90.8% chromosome placement), contig N50 values ranged from 31.1 to 195.8 Mb, with 95.9-99.4% of sequence placed on chromosomes. Gene annotation identified approximately 40,000 gene models per genotype, of which 93.6-93.9% were classified as protein-coding, with 95.9-97.3% complete BUSCOs. Comparison with B73 identified 27,606-30,517 one-to-one syntenic orthologs per genotype, representing 69.4-76.8% of B73 genes. Transposable elements occupied 83.6-88.6% of the genomes, with LTR retrotransposons representing the predominant class. Comparative genome alignments revealed three large inversions, including a 12.65-Mb inversion on chromosome 3 present in six of the 13 lines. Together, these resources expand the genomic representation of maize breeding germplasm and provide a foundation for investigating genetic variation underlying agronomic traits.

papers.title: LuxS Inactivation Increases Antibiotic Susceptibility and Impairs Genetic Competence in Streptococcus pneumoniae
papers.abstract: The LuxS enzyme participates in bacterial metabolism and produces the precursor of autoinducer-2 (AI-2), a signaling molecule implicated in bacterial stress responses and genetic competence. Although LuxS/AI-2 has been associated with antibiotic responses in other streptococci, its contribution to antibiotic susceptibility in Streptococcus pneumoniae remains poorly understood. Here, we investigated the role of LuxS in pneumococcal survival during exposure to erythromycin and ampicillin and examined whether supplementation with 4,5-dihydroxy-2,3-pentanedione (DPD), the precursor of AI-2, could alleviate the effects of luxS inactivation. The {Delta}luxS mutant exhibited significantly greater reductions in viable cell counts than the wild type following antibiotic exposure, even after accounting for differences in baseline growth. Supplementation with 50 nM DPD significantly improved mutant survival during exposure to both antibiotics. We further investigated the contribution of LuxS/AI-2 to genetic competence, a phenotype previously associated with luxS inactivation. The mutant exhibited reduced transformation efficiency, which was significantly improved by DPD supplementation, although recovery remained partial. Together, these findings provide evidence that LuxS contributes to pneumococcal survival during antibiotic exposure and demonstrate that exogenous DPD can partially compensate for the effects of luxS inactivation on antibiotic responses and genetic transformation. These results extend our understanding of LuxS/AI-2-associated phenotypes in S. pneumoniae.

papers.title: Reconstitution in JCVI-syn3B suggests the roles of the Spiroplasma Fibril protein (Sfibril) in swimming
papers.abstract: Spiroplasma, wall-less helical bacteria of the class Mollicutes, swim without flagella by shifting the handedness of their helical body. This motility is driven by an internal ribbon composed of actin-superfamily MreB proteins (SMreB) and the Spiroplasma-specific Fibril protein (Sfibril), which accounts for nearly half of the ribbon mass. However, because helical shape and swimming have been reconstituted with SMreBs alone, the role of Sfibril has remained unclear. Here, we expressed Fibril from Spiroplasma eriocheiris under its native promoter in the minimal synthetic bacterium JCVI-syn3B (syn3), in which swimming had been reconstituted with SMreB proteins, and analyzed cell morphology and swimming. Sfibril formed filaments with chained ring units in syn3 cells and, by itself, induced cell elongation and left-handed helical shape. Elongated cells expressing Sfibril recovered their length after hypo-osmotic shock, indicating that Sfibril confers morphological robustness. In cells expressing SMreB4 and SMreB5 from Spiroplasma, Sfibril increased the fraction of helical and motile cells, extended the distance of continuous kink propagation, reduced cell bending, and increased traveling distance. In addition, Sfibril altered the handedness of SMreB5-driven helices from exclusively right-handed to a mixture of right- and left-handed. These results suggest that Sfibril is not essential for helicity shift but stabilizes the cell body and supports efficient, processive helicity shifts.

papers.title: Charting the Expansive Outer Membrane β-Barrel Landscape in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
papers.abstract: Outer-membrane beta-barrel (OMBB) proteins are central to Gram-negative bacterial physiology, mediating nutrient acquisition and secretion while shaping host interactions and antimicrobial permeability. Yet tools to catalog the diversity and functional potential of the OMBB proteome in these bacteria remain incompletely defined. Here, we combine proteome-scale structure prediction analysis and experimental validation to systematically map the OMBB proteome of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa. We identify 105 proteins containing predicted OMBB domains with 8-26 beta-strands, substantially expanding the repertoire across major structural classes and revealing previously unrecognised domain architectures. Comparison with experimentally defined structures shows that prediction accurately captures global barrel architecture but systematically overestimates beta-strand continuity and underrepresents flexible extracellular loops, key determinants of molecular recognition. We then defined the cryo-EM structures of PA2590 and PA3535 (EprS), confirming their predicted functions as a TonB-dependent transporter and an autotransporter, respectively. Using structural prediction, we also identified the phospholipase A1-like activity in the uncharacterized autotransporter PA4579, linking a predicted catalytic site to function. Together, our findings expand the structural and functional landscape of the P. aeruginosa OMBB proteome and establish a generalizable framework for converting proteome-scale structural predictions into experimentally testable mechanisms, enabling discovery of functions hidden within poorly annotated outer-membrane proteomes.

papers.title: Polymer type and surface functionalization determine the impact of nanoplastics on neural crest cell adhesion, migration, proliferation, and apoptosis in primary cultures.
papers.abstract: Nanoplastics (NP) constitutes a pervasive source of environmental pollution that contaminates all ecosystems, the atmosphere and freshwater. They are absorbed by living organisms and cross biological barriers, with increasing evidence pointing to their harmful effects both at cellular levels and in whole organisms. The impacts of NPs vary not only depending on their size and concentration, but also on the cell type, the polymer composition and surface charge, requiring a comprehensive understanding of the responses of a wide range of cells to these parameters. Because neural crest cells (NCC) are highly proliferative and migratory embryonic progenitors that contribute to a wide range of tissues, they provide a relevant model for investigating the impact of environmental pollutants on developmental cell behaviors. Using a well-established primary NCC culture system, we show that polypropylene (PP) and polyethylene (PE) NPs are more detrimental than polystyrene (PS) NPs to NCC survival and proliferation in a dose-dependent manner. These effects were particularly pronounced for amine-functionalized NPs, which increased NCC apoptosis compared with carboxylate-functionalized NPs. In addition, amine-functionalized PP and PE NPs shortened NCC production period and strongly decrease cell adhesion and migration through alterations of substrate adhesions. Our results indicate that NPs disrupt key biological processes of NCCs, depending on the polymer type and surface functionalization and might contribute to the pathogenesis of structures derived from the NCCs.

papers.title: Extracellular vesicles from alternatively activated macrophages remodel the injured hepatic niche and promote repair
papers.abstract: Alternatively activated macrophages (AAMs) are in clinical development for acute liver injury, but their mechanisms of action remain incompletely understood. AAM therapy remodels the injured hepatic niche, promoting reparative macrophage states, suppressing inflammatory myeloid programmes and restoring hepatocyte metabolic and biosynthetic programmes. We identify extracellular vesicles released by AAMs (AAM-EVs) as essential mediators of AAM therapeutic activity. AAM-EVs enhance macrophage phagocytosis and induce reparative transcriptional and proteomic responses, including increased TREM2 abundance. Following administration in established APAP injury, AAM-EVs reduce necrosis and neutrophilic inflammation, and promote hepatocellular regeneration, and we observe preferential and rapid association of AAM-EVs with hepatic macrophages alongside reparative phenotypic shift. Moreover, pharmacological inhibition of EV release attenuates parent AAM efficacy and TREM2 macrophage accumulation, while EVs derived from Dicer-deficient AAMs exhibit reduced therapeutic activity, implicating miRNA-associated mechanisms. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptomics reveals overlapping but distinct macrophage and hepatocyte responses to AAMs and AAM-EVs. Together, these findings identify EV-mediated communication as an important mechanism of macrophage-induced liver repair and support the development of AAM-EVs as a cell-free therapeutic strategy.

papers.title: Resistome-based machine learning source attribution of a superbug
papers.abstract: Many bacterial human pathogens infect not only humans but also other species, and source attribution has been very useful for studying transmission among the different sources. Yet, critical pathogens such as Acinetobacter baumannii have not been studied using source attribution approaches. Here, we conducted machine source attribution using the resistome of almost 1200 A. baumannii genomes from four sources: humans, companion animals , soil, and white storks. Of note, no other study has used the resistome as input data before. First, we selected the best model among 168 parameter combinations, which was Random Forest, with 5-fold cross-validation and chi2 for feature selection. The model shows a reasonably good accuracy with an F1 weighted score = 0.744, yet class accuracy was dependent on the source. Whereas for companion animals and humans, 93% and 86% of the predictions were correct, respectively; the other two categories (soil and white stork) show correct predictions below 50%. Yet, a core phylogeny and ST assignment reveal that the wrong predictions are associated with multi-host lineages. Finally, we identify the most important ARGs contributing to each class prediction and, in the case of companion animals, tetgenes, which confer resistance to tetracycline, were among the top contributors. Our study shows the resistome's potential for developing models to predict source associations. More broadly, this study shows how integrating machine learning and phylogenomics can help us understand multi-host transmission dynamics.

papers.title: L-Phenylalanine acts as a broad-spectrum plant growth biostimulator for both dicotyledonous and monocotyledonous crops
papers.abstract: L-phenylalanine (Phe), an aromatic amino acid known to induce plant pathogen resistance at concentrations >4 mM, also functions as a broad-spectrum plant growth biostimulator in the total absence of biotic stress. To evaluate its biostimulatory potential, drench and foliar spray applications of Phe (1-16 mM) were tested on dicotyledonous (cucumber, tomato, lettuce) and monocotyledonous (wheat) crops grown under commercial-like net-house conditions with full NPK fertigation (150 mg/ L N). Weekly applications significantly enhanced vegetative growth across all species, increasing plant height by [≥]22-26%, node numbers by [≥]23-40%, and leaf/leaflet area by [≥]36-48% in cucumber and tomato, as well as expanding leaf area in lettuce. In reproductive stages, Phe treatments increased flower initiation, set fruits ([≥]23-27%), total fruit number ([≥]31%), and fruit yield per plant ([≥]30-36%) in cucumber and tomato. In wheat, Phe increased tiller formation, total spike counts by [≥]36%, and fresh/dry plant biomass. Growth enhancement required a strict concentration threshold of [≥]4 mM; lower concentrations (1-2 mM) were inconsistent, and applying 2 mM twice weekly failed to replicate the significant gains of a single 4 mM weekly treatment. Because background fertigation provided a continuous and ample nitrogen supply, periodic trace applications of Phe contributed negligible amounts of nutritional N or C. This supports the conclusion that Phe acts through concentration-dependent physiological and metabolic biostimulation rather than nutrient supplementation.

papers.title: Biased evolution of pollen size after whole genome duplication
papers.abstract: Cell size is an important functional attribute of single-celled organisms, and whole genome duplication (WGD) has long been hypothesized to double the volume of unicells. Pollen of flowering plants is effectively a single-celled organism, comprising the "vegetative cell" of the male gametophyte, which carries the male germline (two sperm cells or their precursor) within its cytoplasm. Instantaneous doubling of evolved pollen size is likely to be excessive, which should bias evolution in young polyploids to size reduction. Here, I test the hypotheses that the magnitude of the effect of WGD on pollen diameter should be doubled volume at inception, and less-than-doubled volume in evolved autotetraploids. Taking data from the literature, I compared 1n = 2x to 1n = 1x pollen diameters in 286 pairs of intraspecific autotetraploids and their diploid progenitors at four successive evolutionary ages: 1) diploid anthers producing some non-reduced pollen, 2) newly formed synthetic or spontaneous autotetraploids, 3) established autotetraploid cultivars, and 4) wild intraspecific autotetraploid cytotypes. Relative to 1x pollen, the volume of 2x non-reduced pollen was at least doubled at inception (31 species), doubled in 65 synthetic and 34 old cultivars, and on average 46% smaller-than-doubled in 54 wild autotetraploid species. Neither 1x pollen size nor 1Cx DNA content of diploids affected the results. Furthermore, wind- versus animal-pollination had little effect. Finally, in 16 autotetraploid-diploid pairs, the differences in pollen size were not correlated with the differences in their 1Cx DNA content. In sum, WGD doubles pollen volume and doubled volume persists in cultivars maintained in benign conditions, but over time in natural conditions, pollen of wild autotetraploids is strongly biased towards reversion to progenitor sizes. Since pollen downsizing after WGD was not matched by genome downsizing, pollen size reduction in young autotetraploids must largely evolve by gene regulation and expression, rather than by a direct relationship between genome size or gene dosage and cell size.

papers.title: Autophagy induction by cytoplasmic Acinus requires Lrrk activity
papers.abstract: Autophagy is a critical pathway for maintaining cellular health in ageing and disease but mechanisms matching levels of autophagy to different stress conditions remain incompletely understood. In response to proteostasis stress, autophagy is induced upon activation of Acinus, a mostly nuclear protein previously linked to alternative splicing as a subunit of the ASAP complex. Here, we show that Acinus induces autophagy independently of its function in splicing. Instead, autophagic flux is promoted by mutations of Acinus that either disrupt its interaction with the ASAP complex or otherwise increase its cytoplasmic fraction. Proximity labeling of the proteome preferentially associated with cytoplasmic rather than nuclear Acinus identified Rab32. Genetic analysis revealed that the Rab32 GTPase and its effector Lrrk kinase are required for autophagy induction by activated Acinus, in contrast to Lrrk-independent mTor-regulated autophagy. This specific requirement in Acinus-regulated autophagy has possible implications for Parkinson's disease for which mutants in the human orthologs of Rab32 and Lrrk constitute risk factors.

papers.title: pH Gradient Drives Redox Reactions in the Nucleolar Caps to Modulate Nucleolar Integrity and Function
papers.abstract: While enzymatic catalysis is the main driver of redox processes in cells, biomolecular condensates exhibit unique electrochemical properties that can potentiate redox reactions. Nevertheless, the regulatory mechanisms governing the electrochemical equilibrium of biomolecular condensates and their influence on the emergent physicochemical functions remain poorly understood. Here, we demonstrate that specific nucleolar stressors induce alkaline nucleolar caps, which generate an interfacial pH gradient and electrical potential that drive spontaneous redox reactions. Non-enzymatic reactive oxygen species (ROS) production depends on positively charged constituents within the nucleolar caps and correlates strongly with the pH microenvironment. Excessive ROS directly modulates the partition and diffusion of proteins rich in redox-sensitive residues, whereas scavenging ROS markedly accelerates the recovery of nucleolar multiphase organization and functionality upon stress removal. Collectively, our findings propose a non-enzymatic redox mechanism operating within cellular condensates and highlight the critical role of physical interfaces in orchestrating the chemical dynamics of biomolecular condensates

papers.title: CCDC81 is a conserved microtubule-binding protein that maintains centriole integrity
papers.abstract: Centrioles are microtubule-based organelles that exhibit a highly conserved architecture that is essential for their function. However, the molecular mechanisms maintaining their structural integrity remain incompletely understood. Here, we characterize CCDC81 as a conserved microtubule-binding protein that contributes to centriole organization. Using expansion microscopy, we localize CCDC81 to the A-C linker of Chlamydomonas basal bodies, where it associates with POC11, the homolog of human A-C linker protein CCDC77. We demonstrate that CCDC81 directly binds microtubules through its N-terminal HU domains, promotes microtubule bundling, and stabilizes microtubules by reducing depolymerization and increasing rescue frequency. Cryo-electron microscopy further reveals its association with the outer microtubule lattice. We identify distinct domains mediating CCDC81 interaction with POC11 and propose a molecular organization of this complex within the A-C linker. Importantly, CCDC81 also localizes to human centrioles, where its depletion disrupts centriole architecture and A-C linker organization, with defects exacerbated by co-depletion of CCDC77. Together, our findings establish CCDC81 as a conserved regulator of microtubule organization and centriole structural integrity.

papers.title: Compartment-associated filtering and environmental gradients shape fungal communities in arid Artemisia species
papers.abstract: Plant-associated fungal communities are shaped by interactions among host, environmental conditions, and compartment-specific filtering processes, yet the relative importance of these drivers remains poorly understood in arid and semi-arid ecosystems. We investigated fungal communities associated with three Artemisia species (Artemisia herba-alba Asso., Artemisia mesatlantica Maire and Artemisia negrei L.), including Moroccan endemics, across bulk soil, rhizosphere, root, and shoot compartments using ITS amplicon sequencing, culture-dependent isolation, and ecological analyses. Fungal community composition differed significantly among compartments (PERMANOVA, R2 = 0.08, P = 0.012), whereas alpha diversity showed limited variation. Taxonomic profiles revealed compartment-associated shifts, with recurrent fungal genera concentrated in belowground compartments and a higher proportion of unclassified taxa in shoots. Core microbiome analyses identified overlapping fungal taxa between rhizosphere and root communities. Soil physicochemical gradients were associated with fungal community composition, and structural equation modeling indicated significant associations with both environmental variables and plant compartments. Source-tracking analysis attributed approximately 99.4% of root community composition to rhizosphere sources, whereas shoot communities showed contributions from both roots (60%) and the rhizosphere (39%). Culture-dependent isolation recovered 21 fungal isolates, with five genera shared between cultivation and sequencing datasets. Together, these findings reveal compartment-associated fungal community restructuring along the soil?plant continuum and highlight the complementary contributions of environmental conditions, plant-associated habitats, and cultivation-based characterization to understanding fungal microbiomes in arid ecosystems.
